title: "Visualizing data"

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(cowplot)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

x <- read.csv("../data/Focal_Bird_Morphology.csv")
xname <- data.frame(species = tolower(c("JAWE", "RBLE",
                                        "RVBU", "RWBU",
                                        "WRSH")),
                    full_name = c("Japanese white-eye", "red-billed leiothrix",
                                  "red-vented bulbul", "red-whiskered bulbul",
                                  "white-rumped shama"))

x <- full_join(x, xname)
```

[kuhikuhi]{.alert}

## Learning goals

1. Understand how variable types determine figure design
2. Distinguish between [exploratory]{.alert} and [explanatory]{.alert} figures
3. Identify what makes a good graph
4. Identify best practices in figure design
5. Identify misleading graphics and fix them


## 1. Understand how variable types determine figure design

We use the *R* package `ggplot2` for figure design

The basic building blocks are:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = "the data.frame we're plotting",
       mapping = aes(x = "column with data for x-axis",
                     y = "column with data for y-axis")) +
    geom_"type of plot"
```

## 1. Understand how variable types determine figure design

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

**Explanatory:** Numerical

**Response:** Numerical

**Figure:** Scatter plot

<br>

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point()
```
:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "5in"
#| fig-align: center

set.seed(200)
dat <- data.frame(treatment = rep(LETTERS[1:3], c(12, 30, 18)))

dat$type <- as.factor(dat$treatment) |>
    as.numeric() |>
    rnorm(nrow(dat), mean = _) |>
    cut(breaks = 4) |>
    as.numeric() |>
    (\(x) paste0("type_0", x))()

dat$x <- runif(nrow(dat), 0, 20)
dat$y <- 0.5 * dat$x + 4 * as.numeric(as.factor(dat$treatment)) + 
    rnorm(nrow(dat))



ggplot(dat, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point()
```

:::

:::


## 1. Understand how variable types determine figure design

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
**Explanatory:** Categorical *or* Ordinal

**Response:** Numerical

**Figure:** Jitter plot

<br>

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

ggplot(data, aes(x = treatment, y = y, 
                color = treatment)) +
    geom_jitter() 
```

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "5in"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(dat, aes(x = treatment, y = y, color = treatment)) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.25) +
    scale_color_viridis_d() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```

:::
:::

## 1. Understand how variable types determine figure design

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

**Explanatory:** Categorical *or* Ordinal

**Response:** Numerical

**Figure:** Jitter plot ***or*** [*box plot*]{.underline}

<br>

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

ggplot(data, aes(x = treatment, y = y, 
                 fill = treatment)) +
    geom_boxplot()

```

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "5in"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(dat, aes(x = treatment, y = y, fill = treatment)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    scale_fill_viridis_d() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

```
:::
:::

## 1. Understand how variable types determine figure design

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

**Explanatory:** Categorical *or* Ordinal

**Response:** Categorical *or* Ordinal

**Figure:** Stacked bar plot

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false


ggplot(data, aes(x = treatment, 
                fill = type)) +
    geom_bar() 

```

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "5in"
#| fig-align: center


ggplot(dat, aes(x = treatment, fill = type)) +
    geom_bar() +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "inferno")

```

:::
:::

## 1. Understand how variable types determine figure design

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

**Explanatory:** Categorical *or* Ordinal

**Response:** Categorical *or* Ordinal

**Figure:** Stacked bar plot (scaled to proportion)

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false


ggplot(data, aes(x = treatment, 
                fill = type)) +
    geom_bar(position = "fill") 

```

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "5in"
#| fig-align: center


ggplot(dat, aes(x = treatment, fill = type)) +
    geom_bar(position = "fill") +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "inferno") +
    ylab("Proportion")

```

:::
:::



## 1. Understand how variable types determine figure design

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
**Explanatory:** "none" (i.e. you just want to check out response)

**Response:** Numerical

**Figure:** Histogram

<br>

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

ggplot(data, aes(x = y)) +
    geom_histogram()

```


:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "5in"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(dat, aes(x = y)) +
    geom_histogram()

```

:::
:::

## 2. Distinguish between [exploratory]{.alert} and [explanatory]{.alert} figures

For [exploratory plots]{.alert}: Don't worry about pretty colors, labels, names, etc. The goal is for you to understand the data.

For [explanatory plots]{.alert}: Focus on all of this. You must consider your audience may, for example, consist of:

- People unfamiliar with your data
- People with different vision, and/or black-and-white printing

## 2. Distinguish between [exploratory]{.alert} and [explanatory]{.alert} figures

Let's use an example

```{r, echo = TRUE}
# Data on morphology of some non-native birds in Hawaiʻi
# from Gleditsch & Sperry (2020) *Ecology and Evolution*
birds <- read.csv("../data/bird_morpho.csv")
head(birds)
```

## 2. Distinguish between [exploratory]{.alert} and [explanatory]{.alert} figures

```{r}
gp1 <- ggplot(birds, aes(x = mass, y = wing)) +
    geom_point()


gp2 <- ggplot(birds, aes(x = mass, y = wing)) +
    geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.5) +
    xlab("Body mass (g)") +
    ylab("Wing length (mm)") +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
          axis.title = element_text(size = 20))
```

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**[Exploratory]{.alert}**

```{r, fig.asp = 1, fig.width = 4}
gp1
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**[Explanatory]{.alert}**

```{r, fig.asp = 1, fig.width = 4}
gp2
```
:::
:::

## 2. Distinguish between [exploratory]{.alert} and [explanatory]{.alert} figures

Contrast code using **ggplot2** (we fully explain in Lab 02)

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**[Exploratory]{.alert}**

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
# minimal code needed
ggplot(birds, aes(x = mass, y = wing)) +
    geom_point()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**[Explanatory]{.alert}**

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
# plenty more code needed
ggplot(birds, aes(x = mass, y = wing)) +
    geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.5) +
    xlab("Body mass (g)") +
    ylab("Wing length (mm)") +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
                se = FALSE) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
          axis.title = element_text(size = 20))
```
:::
:::


## Four keys of good data visualization

1. Show the data
2. Make patterns in the data easy to see
3. Represent magnitudes honestly
4. Display graphical elements clearly

## Mistake 1: Hide the data

How to hide data:

- Provide only statistical summaries
- Over-plotting

::: {.fragment}

How to show data:

- Present all of the data points, while allowing all to be seen

:::

## Mistake 1: Hide the data

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}

This plot hides the variation within species

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "7in"
#| fig-align: center

bd <- birds[birds$species %in% c("rwbu", "wrsh", "jawe"), ]

ggplot(bd, aes(x = full_name, y = mass, fill = full_name)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean") +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab("") + ylab("Mass (g)") +
    scale_fill_viridis_d() +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) {
        strwrap(x, width = 10, simplify = FALSE) |>
            sapply(FUN = paste, collapse = "\n")
    })
```

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}

This plot hides the density of observations

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "7in"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(bd, aes(x = full_name, y = mass, color = species)) +
    geom_point() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab("") + ylab("Mass (g)") +
    scale_color_viridis_d() +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) {
        strwrap(x, width = 10, simplify = FALSE) |>
            sapply(FUN = paste, collapse = "\n")
    })
```

:::

::: {.fragment}

**Fixed!** This plot shows all of the observations

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "7in"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(bd, aes(x = full_name, y = mass, color = species)) +
    geom_jitter(alpha = 0.5) +
    scale_color_viridis_d() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab("") + ylab("Mass (g)") +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) {
        strwrap(x, width = 10, simplify = FALSE) |>
            sapply(FUN = paste, collapse = "\n")
    })
```

:::

:::

## Mistake 2: Make patterns hard to see

How to hide patterns:

- Make one plot and call it good
- Use unreasonable scales
- Arrange factors nonsensically

::: {.fragment}

How to make patterns in the data easy to see:

- Choose the best from multiple potential plots
- Use appropriate scales
- Arrange factors meaningfully

:::


## Mistake 2: Make patterns hard to see

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}

Non-intuitive ordering of categories hides patterns

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "6.5in"
#| fig-align: center

d <- data.frame(Treatment = rep(c("control", "low dose", "high dose"),
                            each = 20))

set.seed(123)

d$Response <- rnorm(nrow(d))

d$Response[d$Treatment == "control"] <-
    d$Response[d$Treatment == "control"] + 3
d$Response[d$Treatment == "low dose"] <-
    d$Response[d$Treatment == "low dose"] + 8

d$Response[d$Treatment == "high dose"] <-
    d$Response[d$Treatment == "high dose"] + 10

pal <- hsv(c(0.08, 0.12, 0.8),
           c(1.0, 0.7, 1.0),
           c(0.8, 0.9, 0.4))
ggplot(d, aes(Treatment, Response, color = Treatment)) +
    geom_jitter() +
    scale_color_manual(values = pal[c(3, 1, 2)]) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}

*Fixed!* Intuitive ordering of categories emphasizes patterns

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "6.5in"
#| fig-align: center

d$Treatment <- factor(d$Treatment,
                      levels = c("control", "low dose", "high dose"))
gtrial <- ggplot(d, aes(Treatment, Response, color = Treatment)) +
    geom_jitter() +
    scale_color_manual(values = pal[c(3, 1, 2)]) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

gtrial
```

:::

::: {.fragment}

*Broken again!* Poorly chosen scale hides patterns

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "6.5in"
#| fig-align: center

gtrial_bad_scale <- gtrial + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100))

gtrial_bad_scale
```

:::

:::

## Mistake 3: Display Magnitudes Dishonestly

How to represent magnitudes *dis*honestly:

- Starting/stopping axes at arbitrary values

::: {.fragment}

How to represent magnitudes *honestly*:

- Don't do that!

:::

We've already seen this once

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "6.5in"
#| fig-align: center

gtrial_bad_scale
```

## Mistake 4: Display graphical elements unclearly

How to display graphical elements unclearly:

- Accept default plotting options
- Do not consider how a diverse audience will interpret your figure

::: {.fragment}

How to display graphical elements clearly:

- Reflect on plot design
    - Are labels big enough?
    - Can all elements be clearly seen?
    - Is sizing and spacing appropriate?
- Consider diverse audiences and how they will interact with your plot

:::

## Mistake 4: Display graphical elements unclearly

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}

Can you read the x-axis?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "6in"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(birds, aes(x = full_name)) +
    geom_bar() +
    xlab("") +
    ylab("Sample size")
```

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}

Flipping improves readability

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2.25
#| out-width: "8in"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(birds, aes(y = full_name)) +
    geom_bar() +
    xlab("Sample size") +
    ylab("")
```

:::

::: {.fragment}

Flipping improves readability...and we should probably re-order

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2.25
#| out-width: "8in"
#| fig-align: center

birds$full_name <- factor(birds$full_name,
                          levels = names(sort(table(birds$full_name))))
ggplot(birds, aes(y = full_name)) +
    geom_bar() +
    xlab("Sample size") +
    ylab("")
```

:::

:::

## Mistake 4: Display graphical elements unclearly

Consider colorblindness

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4

gp3 <- ggplot(bd, aes(x = mass, y = wing, color = species)) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    xlab("Body mass (g)") +
    ylab("Wing length (mm)") +
    # theme_cowplot() +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
          axis.title = element_text(size = 20),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 18),
          legend.title = element_text(size = 18),
          plot.title = element_text(size = 20),
          legend.position = c(0.8, 0.22))


plot_grid(
    gp3 + ggtitle("no color blindness"),
    gp3 + scale_color_manual(values = c("#A59A71", "#908048", "#768FF5")) +
        ggtitle("red-green"),
    gp3 + scale_color_manual(values = c("#ED7377", "#51B293", "#60ADB7")) +
        ggtitle("blue-yellow"),
    nrow = 1
)
```

## Mistake 4: Display graphical elements unclearly

*The fix: consider color carefully*

::: {.fragment}

`ggplot2` provides powerful methods for working with colors

:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

::: {.fragment}

...yet the defaults are ***rubbish***

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4

gp3
```

:::

:::

::: {.column}

::: {.fragment}

we have to explicitly set good colors

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4

gp3 +
    scale_color_viridis_d()
```

:::

:::

:::
